blocks.text: But aljarbuo is also said to devise something else. At times it covers its windows, or more truly its openings, with earth on the topmost surface, so that they do not appear from outside ^{(10)}. In Arabic this is called دم damma [damma]. Alcamus: دم اليربوع حجره غطاه وسواه [damma al-yarbūʿ ḥajrahu ghaṭṭāhu wa-sawwāhu] Damma aljarbuo, he covered his lair and levelled it. Hence the lair also has the name دممة dumama [dumama]. The same Alcamus: الدممة حجرة اليربوع وتراب يجمعه اليربوع ويخرجه من الحجر فيسوي به بابه [al-dumama ḥujrat al-yarbūʿ wa-turāb yajmaʿuhu al-yarbūʿ wa-yukhrijuhu min al-ḥajar fa-yusawwī bihi bābahu] Dumama, the lair of aljarbuo, and the earth which it gathers and digs out of its lair in order to level its entrance. Accordingly, as the opening of its lair, covered over with earth, is called نافقا naphika [nāfiqāʾ], from this a metaphor is taken: نافق naphaka [nāfaqa], a verb of the third form, means to dissemble in religion, and to profess one thing with the mouth while keeping another hidden in the mind. And منافق munaphik [munāfiq] is a hypocrite. Damir: ظاهر بيته تراب وباطنه حفر وكذلك المنافق ظاهره ايمان وباطنه كفر [ẓāhir baytihi turāb wa-bāṭinuhu ḥufar wa-kadhālika al-munāfiq ẓāhiruhu īmān wa-bāṭinuhu kufr] The outer part of its house is earth, but the inner part is hollow. In the same way the hypocrite has faith on the outside, but unbelief on the inside. Algiahid and others: واسم المنافق لم يكن في الجاهلية لكن لمن اسر الكفر واظهر الايمان [wa-ism al-munāfiq lam yakun fī l-jāhiliyya lākin li-man asarra l-kufr wa-aẓhara l-īmān] The name munaphik did not exist in paganism, but it is said of the one who conceals unbelief and displays faith. Albazi: تعالي اشتق له هذا الاسم من هذا الاصل وهو من نافقا اليربوع لانه لما ابطن الكفر [taʿālā ishtaqqa lahu hādhā l-ism min hādhā l-aṣl wa-huwa min nāfiqāʾ al-yarbūʿ li-annahu lammā abṭana l-kufr] [col. 1013] واظهر الايمان [wa-aẓhara l-īmān] God Most High derived the name of the hypocrite from this root, namely from naphika, or the opening of the mouse called aljarbuo; because inside is unbelief and outside is faith. The Arabs say this and much more on Azoara 73 of the Qur'an, whose title is المنافقون [al-munāfiqūn], the hypocrites. In Alcamus the nest of this animal is called لغز [lughz] [II, 424] logoz, as if you were to say labyrinth, because in nests of this kind the passages are winding and extremely intricate. And accordingly in Arabic الغاز [alghāz] algaz is used of طرق تلطوي وتشكل علي مسالكها [ṭuruq talṭawī wa-tashkul ʿalā masālikihā] paths which are twisted and tangled along their course. To this kind of mouse must be referred what Synesius says of a certain commander John, near the end of Letter 104: Δίκην ἀρουραίου μυὸς ἐνεδεδύκει τῇ πέτρᾳ [dikēn arouraiou myos enededykei tē petra], Like a field mouse he had hidden himself in the rock, that is, in Bombaea, a fortress very strongly fortified in a hollow of the rock. For no other field mice make their nests in rock, but only aljarbuo ^{(11)}. Ibnolgiauzi confirms this: اليربوع لا يتخذ بيته الا في موضع صلب مرتفع ليسلم من سيل او حافر ثم لا يجعلة الا عند اكمة او شجرة او صخرة ليلا يضل اذا عاد اليه [al-yarbūʿ lā yattakhidhu baytahu illā fī mawḍiʿ ṣulb murtafiʿ li-yaslama min sayl aw ḥāfir thumma lā yajʿaluhu illā ʿinda akama aw shajara aw ṣakhra li-allā yaḍilla idhā ʿāda ilayhi] Aljarbuo does not make its house except in a hard place (that is, rocky) and elevated, so as to be safe from the inflow of waters and from the hoof (of horses). And it does not set it up except at mounds, or trees, or rocks, lest it go astray when it returns to it. This happens above all to the young of this little animal. Hence a proverb in Damir: اضل من ولد اليربوع [aḍall min walad al-yarbūʿ] More lost than the young of aljarbuo, said of one who wanders and nowhere sets foot firmly. In the same place: وفي طباعه انه اذا مشي في ارض سهلة او لينة مشي علي موخر كفه حتي لا يعرف اثر وطيه كما يفعل الارنب [wa-fī ṭibāʿihi annahu idhā mashā fī arḍ sahla aw layyina mashā ʿalā mu'akhkhar kaffihi ḥattā lā yuʿrafa athar waṭʾihi kamā yafʿal al-arnab] It is also part of its nature that, when it walks on soft and tender ground, it stands on the tips of its feet, so that its tracks may not be recognized in the places it has trodden; this is also the habit of the hare. Likewise: وهو [II, 425] يجتر ويبعر وله كرش واسنان واضراس من الفك الاعلي والاسفلي [yajtarr wa-yabʿar wa-lahu karsh wa-asnān wa-aḍrās min al-fakk al-aʿlā wa-l-asfal] It also ruminates, and drops dung, and has a paunch (like ruminants), although it has incisors and molars, both in the upper and in the lower jaw. The same mouse has this peculiarity, that it leaps. The Arabs express this by the very appropriate verb بحظل bachdala [baḥẓala]. Alcamus: بحظل قفز قفزان اليربوع [baḥẓala qafaza qafazān al-yarbūʿ] Bachdala, he leaped with the leap of aljarbuo. So also Giauhari. Theophrastus observed the very same above of those mice which walk on two feet: Ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι [Hotan de diōkōntai, pēdōsi]; if anyone pursues them, they leap. In its lairs a kind of snake makes its nest, which the Arabs call جنادع gianadio [junādiʿ], or جنادب gianadibo [janādib]. Alcamus: الجنادع الاجناش اوجنادب تكون في حجرة اليرابيع [al-junādiʿ al-ajnāsh aw janādib takūn fī ḥujrat al-yarābīʿ] Algianadio, a (kind of) serpents, or gia- [col. 1014] nadibo: these are in the nest of aljarabii, which is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. If aljarbuo mates with the common mouse, the hybrid mouse born from it is called فرنب [farnab] pharnab, or phirnib. Alcamus: الفرنب الفارة او ولدها من اليربوع [al-farnab al-fāra aw waladuhā min al-yarbūʿ] Alpharnab (or alphirnib) is a mouse, or its offspring from aljarbuo. This too is peculiar to it, that aljarbuo is eaten by the Arabs, although otherwise the eating of a mouse is forbidden to them. Damir, in the chapter الفار [al-fār] alphar, that is, On the mouse: يحرم اكل جميع انواع الفار الا اليربوع [yuḥarram akl jamīʿ anwāʿ al-fār illā l-yarbūʿ] The eating of all species of mouse is forbidden, except aljarbuo. There is, however, some disagreement among the Arabs on this matter. For according to the opinion of Abuchaniphas: لا يوكل لانه من الحشرات [lā yuʾkal li-annahu min al-ḥasharāt] It is not eaten (aljarbuo); because it is one of the subterranean animals. And Algazali, in the book whose title is الوسيط [al-Wasīṭ] The Mediator, denies that anything is to be eaten من الحشرات الا الضب [min al-ḥasharāt illā l-ḍabb] of the subterranean animals except the land crocodile. Yet others make further exceptions: اليربوع وابن عرس وام حبين والقنفد والدلدل [al-yarbūʿ wa-ibn ʿirs wa-umm ḥubayn wa-l-qunfudh wa-l-duldul] aljarbuo, and the weasel, and the chameleon, and the hedgehog, and the porcupine. Hence of aljarbuo Damir says: يحل اكله لان العرب تستطيبه وتحله [yaḥillu aklahu li-anna l-ʿarab tastaṭībuhu wa-taḥilluhu] Its eating is permitted; because the Arabs allow it and take delight in it. So, evidently, the great Canonists of the Arabs decide: Ata, and Achmed Ben-Hantal, and Ibnolmandsar, and Abutsaur, etc. Accordingly not only aljarbuo but also its lair is bought, that is, the right of searching and scrutinizing it so that the animal may be caught in it. Because this mostly meets with little success, it has passed into a proverb among the Arabs, as when they say: كالمشتري القاصعا باليربوع [ka-l-mushtarī al-qāṣiʿāʾ bi-l-yarbūʿ] Like one who, instead of [II, 426] aljarbuo, buys its hole. This proverb يضرب الذي يدع العين ويتبع الاثر [yuḍrab li-lladhī yadaʿ al-ʿayn wa-yattabiʿ al-athar] strikes the one who, leaving the spring, follows only the trail. In Greek you might say, Σκιὰν ἀντὶ τοῦ σώματος [Skian anti tou sōmatos], A shadow instead of the body. And here too the Arabs are dainty, and among the other mice of this kind they prefer the Suphariensis, which Alcamus describes thus: يربوع شفاري ضخم الاذنين وطويلهما العاري البراثين ولا يلحق سريعا والطويل والغوايم الرخو اللحم الدسم [yarbūʿ shafārī ḍakhm al-udhunayn wa-ṭawīluhumā al-ʿārī al-barāthin wa-lā yulḥaq sarīʿan wa-l-ṭawīl wa-l-ghawāyim al-rakhw al-laḥm al-dasim] The Suphariensis jarbuo has thick and long ears, is bare in its claws, so that it is not easily caught, has long feet, and tender and fat flesh. In Abenbitar: يربوع الاسراييلي لحم اليربوع يقد وغذا كثير ويلين البطن [yarbūʿ al-isrāʾīlī laḥm al-yarbūʿ yuqadd wa-ghidhāʾ kathīr wa-yulayyin al-baṭn] Iarbuo Israëliticus is the name; the flesh of aljarbuo is dried. It is, moreover, very nourishing, and loosens the bowels. To dry in Arabic is قد kadda [qadda], which properly signi- [col. 1015] fies to expose to the wind flesh cut lengthwise, as among us to smoke, so that the moisture is drawn off. Hence قداد kedad [qidād] is used both of the hedgehog and of aljarbuo; because each animal is dried in this way. Alkamus: القداد القنفد واليربوع [al-qidād al-qunfudh wa-l-yarbūʿ] Alkedado: the hedgehog and Aljarbuo. In the Arabic versions of the Sacred text the word aljarbuo occurs only once in all, namely Isa. LXVI, 17, where the Arabic translator has: الذين ياكلون لحم الخنازير والرذالات واليربوع [alladhīna yaʾkulūna laḥm al-khanāzīr wa-l-radhālāt wa-l-yarbūʿ] Those who eat the flesh of swine, and abominations, and Aljarbua, that is, the species for the genus. For the Hebrew has והעכבר, and the mouse. But the Arab had a reason for rendering اليربوع aljarbua [al-yarbūʿ]. For we have already taught that in the whole genus of mice this one alone is edible among the Arabs. Besides, although עכבר achbar in Hebrew means mouse in general, yet in Arabic this very word عكبر achbar [ʿakbar], in the plural عكابر achabiro [ʿakābir], means the male of اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbui. Alcamus: العكابر ذكور من اليرابيع [al-ʿakābir dhukūr min al-yarābīʿ] Alachabiro, the males of the Aljarabii: which, as we have already said, is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. So since اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] is the name of the species, العكبر [al-ʿakbar] alachbar means the male, as العطيوطة [al-ʿaṭīṭa] alatiuta the female. Alcamus: العطيوطة اليربوع الانثي [al-ʿaṭīṭa al-yarbūʿ al-unthā] Alatiuta, the female Aljarbuo. Teixeira the Portuguese calls them ratones del mato, that is, mice of the thicket, and describes them in these words in Indici itinerarii chapter 4: Son estos ratones del grandor de los grandes nuestros communes, tienen el pelo pardo tirante à blanco. Tienen de raton las orejas, manos, y la cola: cuya punta, y los ojos, y cabeça, son de conejo; y las piernas como de gazela. Corren mucho saltando, hazen cueua como conejo. Y ay dellos grande quantidad [II, 427] por aquel de sierto. Los Arabes los comen, y dizen, que son muy buenos. That is: These mice are equal in size to the largest of the common ones, of a greyish colour. They have the small ears, forefeet and tail of a mouse; but the tip of the tail, the eyes and the head are those of a rabbit; and the haunches (that is, hind legs) those of a gazelle. They mostly run by leaping, and dig burrows as rabbits do. Of these in that desert (in the part of Arabia near Babylonia) there is a very great number. The Arabs use them for food, and assert that they are of excellent flavour. In these words aljarbuo is described completely, as everyone will admit. Of the same Olearius speaks thus in book 6 of the Persian Itinerary, page 64: Near Terkin (in Circassia) we saw a kind of field mouse, called in Arabic IERBUA. It has the size of a squirrel, and is not dissimilar in form; but its fur is darker; and its head is that of a mouse; its ears are long; its legs short in front, longer behind. Consequently they run only uphill; on level ground they mostly creep, or are carried by a leap five or six feet above the ground. The tail is long, lying along the back, bare on the stem, and hairy and whitish at the tip. To see many leaping upward with the same impetus was a pleasant sight. They say that Babylonia and Arabia swarm with them, and that they are food for the inhabitants. There are some that move from the fields into houses and steal money.
